explanation: The photostress recovery test helps to diﬀerentiate between retinopathies and optic neuropathies by testing the amount of time it takes for vision to recover after being stimulated with a bright light. The photostress recovery test requires a corrected distance visual acuity of 20/80 or better. The patient is tested monocularly, gazing into a bright light held 2-3 cm from the eye for 10 seconds. Immediately after the light stimulus is removed, the patient attempts to read the next larger Snellen visual acuity line above the previously measured corrected visual acuity (eg, if the patient's corrected visual acuity is 20/25, the 20/30 line would be measured). Normal photostress recovery time is less than 30 seconds, but patients with maculopathy or severe carotid artery stenosis have prolonged recovery times (≥ 90-180 seconds). By contrast, patients with optic neuropathy have normal photostress recovery times. explanation: The clinical scenario is most consistent with papilledema, which is optic nerve head edema resulting from increased intracranial pressure (ICP). On ophthalmoscopy, papilledema is indistinguishable from other causes of optic nerve head edema. Suspicion of papilledema warrants urgent brain imaging, ideally MRI and magnetic resonance venography of the brain and orbits with contrast, to rule out an intracranial mass lesion and cerebral venous thrombosis. Normal brain imaging results should prompt evaluation of the cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) pressure and composition by lumbar puncture. Observation is not recommended when there is suspicion of papilledema, because chronic papilledema can result in permanent visual loss. There are several radiographic features that might suggest increased intracranial pressure; however, after normal brain imaging, a lumbar puncture with opening pressure and CSF studies should be performed next. Acetazolamide is the ﬁrst-line medical treatment for idiopathic intracranial hypertension. However, treatment without conﬁrmation of the diagnosis by neuroimaging and lumbar puncture is not recommended.

Although this patient has no systemic symptoms, the optic disc appearance on the left is suggestive of infarction that occurs in the setting of vasculitis, and in this patient, with very high ESR and CRP, the most common type of vasculitis would be giant cell arteritis. A temporal artery biopsy should be performed, but treatment with corticosteroids should not be delayed to obtain the biopsy. In giant cell arteritis, the ESR and CRP can be both highly elevated despite no systemic symptoms (so-called occult GCA). Up to 16% of cases of GCA may have normal ESR levels. When arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AAION) due to GCA is suspected, immediate initiation of high-dose corticosteroid therapy is crucial. It is estimated that with observation, 50% or more of patients will lose vision in the initially unaﬀected eye within 1 week. Additional tests with carotid ultrasonography and neuroimaging would not be necessary if the biopsy was positive and should not be done in advance of treatment with corticosteroids. When patients present with GCA and vision loss in 1 eye, it is often recommended to use high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day for the ﬁrst 3-5 days). Tapering of steroid treatment should be slow; there can be a risk of recurrence (7%) in either the same or the other eye during withdrawal.

explanation: Syphilitic uveitis is considered a CNS disease and warrants a lumbar puncture in all cases. A positive CSF VDRL is diagnostic for neurosyphilis. question: A patient has the ﬁnding shown in the ﬁgure. What results are most likely on visual ﬁeld testing?
explanation: The ﬁnding of ptosis with an adduction, elevation, and depression deﬁcit is highly suggestive of a third nerve palsy. The addition of a contralateral weakness is indicative of a midbrain lesion aﬀecting the third nerve fascicle and the cerebral peduncle, resulting in an ipsilateral third nerve palsy and contralateral weakness (Weber syndrome). A lesion within the interpeduncular cistern, cavernous sinus, or orbital apex can cause a third nerve palsy, but it would not be expected to cause contralateral weakness.

question: A 73-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with acute onset diplopia and ptosis. Examination shows right eyelid ptosis and a deﬁcit in adduction, elevation, and depression in the right eye. In addition, the patient has a weakness of her left extremities that started at the time of the diplopia and ptosis. Based on the clinical ﬁndings, where is the lesion?
explanation: The correct answer is pseudo-Foster-Kennedy syndrome. Foster- Kennedy syndrome occurs when an intracranial mass on 1 side compresses the ipsilateral optic nerve, causing optic atrophy and thus optic nerve pallor, while also raising the intracranial pressure and causing the contralateral disc to swell. The normal MRI in the question rules this possibility out. Pseudo-Foster-Kennedy syndrome is caused by bilateral, sequential attacks of nonarteritic ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). The ﬁrst nerve aﬀected becomes pale 4-8 weeks after the attack, and thus, when the second optic nerve becomes aﬀected and acutely swollen, it yields the same appearance as Foster-Kennedy syndrome, with 1 optic nerve showing pallor and the other nerve showing edema. The 5-year risk for involvement of the fellow eye in NAION is approximately 15%. Untreated giant cell arteritis (GCA) could indeed cause bilateral disc swelling and optic nerve pallor; however, GCA left untreated for several months would be expected to have caused much more profound vision loss. It was also noted that review of systems was negative, also making GCA less likely. This patient is diabetic, making diabetic papillopathy a consideration; however, the optic nerves are typically hyperemic in diabetic papillopathy, and approximately half of patients show prominent surface telangiectasias that are often mistaken for neovascularization of the disc. In addition, the majority (63%-80%) of patients with diabetic papillopathy have diabetic retinopathy, which this patient does not have.

explanation: This case describes a woman with divergence insuﬃciency secondary to sagging eye syndrome. Sagging eye syndrome is caused by degeneration of the lateral rectus- superior rectus band, leading to inferior displacement of the lateral rectus muscle. Patients develop diplopia due to a comitant esodeviation greater at distance than at near vision (usually orthophoric at near). While lateral eye movements remain full, there may be some limitation of supraduction, which can be asymmetric in some cases. In addition to the divergence insuﬃciency pattern esotropia, sagging eye syndrome often is associated with deep superior sulci, high lid creases, and ptosis from levator dehiscence. Since the esotropia is comitant and no worse in abduction (which would suggest a sixth nerve palsy), as well as being found in isolation, it is likely benign and can be treated optically with base-out prism over distance spectacles. Strabismus surgery is another treatment option. The incorrect answer choices address the diﬀerential diagnosis of new-onset esotropia: myasthenia gravis, which can be treated with pyridostigmine; Graves disease, in which the thyroid hormone abnormality can be treated by decreasing the thyroid antibody response with methimazole; and, in patients over 50 years old, giant cell arteritis, which is treated with high-dose steroid. ischemia.

explanation: When the pupil function is completely normal (ie, equal pupil size and reactivity) but there is complete loss of eyelid and ocular motor function of the third nerve, this represents a typical ﬁnding of ischemic (microvascular) cranial neuropathy. Other associated ﬁndings can include pain. Ischemic diseases associated with this include diabetes mellitus, hypertension, or hyperlipidemia. Neuroimaging may not be required immediately, depending on comorbid conditions; however, failure to recover after 3 months warrants investigation to rule out other possibilities, such as a mass or inﬁltrative lesion. If there is relative pupil sparing, the pupil may react normally with only minimal impairment of levator palpebrae and extraocular function. When this occurs, other ﬁbers within the third cranial nerve are spared and usually related to compressive lesions and can later progress to involve the pupil. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits using a gadolinium contrast agent and with attention to the path of the aﬀected third nerve should be obtained.

explanation: The patient has ptosis and a smaller pupil on the left indicative of a lesion to the oculosympathetic pathway, resulting in a left Horner syndrome. Other ﬁndings in a Horner syndrome are the presence of anisocoria that is greater in dim light than in bright light, dilation lag of the aﬀected pupil, lower lid ptosis (rising of the lower lid), and anhidrosis of the ipsilateral face. Horner syndrome can be conﬁrmed with pharmacologic testing. Cocaine blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine released at sympathetic nerve terminals in the eye, causing pupillary dilation, eyelid retraction, and conjunctival blanching in the unaﬀected eye. With Horner syndrome, little or no norepinephrine is released into the synaptic cleft. Therefore, cocaine has no eﬀect, and the miotic pupil remains unchanged. A postcocaine anisocoria of 1 mm or more is diagnostic of Horner syndrome on the side of the smaller pupil. Topical apraclonidine can also be used to conﬁrm Horner syndrome. A pupil with Horner syndrome will dilate in response to topical apraclonidine (weak alpha1-adrenergic agonist) because of iris dilator supersensitivity that develops several days after injury to the sympathetic pathway.

question: A 37-year-old man complains of new onset anisocoria. His right pupil is 4.0 mm, and his left is 3.0 mm. His right palpebral ﬁssure is 11 mm, while his left is 9.5 mm. What test would conﬁrm an oculosympathetic paresis on the left side?
explanation: This patient has signs of a left optic neuropathy (left RAPD), aﬀecting at least the left cranial nerves (CNs III, V1, and VI), based on the ﬁndings of ptosis, limited ductions in all directions, and decreased corneal sensation. The combination of CN II and ophthalmoplegia localizes to the orbital apex. If CN II is unaﬀected, the location of the lesion would be expected in the ipsilateral cavernous sinus. The hallmark of ophthalmoplegia secondary to a lesion of the cavernous sinus is ipsilateral ocular motor nerve dysfunction involving any combination of third, fourth, ﬁfth, and sixth CNs and sympathetic ﬁbers. The oﬀending lesion may extend toward the optic foramen or into the orbital apex, in which case optic nerve function can be compromised. The designation orbital apex syndrome is then applied. A brain stem lesion can cause various craniopathies, but would not be expected to cause an optic neuropathy. A cortical lesion would not be expected to cause an optic neuropathy or unilateral ophthalmoplegia. They decalcify.

explanation: The patient is reporting symptoms suspicious for superior oblique myokymia, which is characterized by monocular, paroxysmal, high-frequency bursts of superior oblique contraction. The resulting eye movements are of very small amplitude and usually require magniﬁcation (such as at the slit lamp or with a 20 D lens) for observation. Many conditions, including ocular myasthenia gravis and decompensated phorias, may produce ﬂeeting double vision. In these cases, patients do not experience the tremulous ocular sensation that is present with superior oblique myokymia. The diagnosis may be challenging unless an episode is observed, and high clinical suspicion is required once alternative diagnoses are excluded with motility and cover testing.
